title: Picture it, tag its value
header_line: My analysis of one book on habits. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: How vividly can you picture what you want to do?

I said that elevating emotion sets an anchor, whether the event is imagined or not. I gave the example of a child who hears gossip that a best friend spoke badly of them, gets upset, summons the courage to confront the friend, and learns it was not true. The imagined event was as emotional as a real one.

A student asked why that works. I answered with a visualization: picture yourself thirsty, opening the refrigerator, grabbing a jar of water. What color is the jar, which hand? Your imagination created that reality.
I said that the more emotionally engaging it is, the more likely you are to commit to the intention.

I said it is called value tagging: you determine the importance of some information. If something is important, such as a big deal, your emotional engagement is high, so your focus, visualization and imagination are high.

A student said: the more you think about it, the more you create paths and decision trees to the outcome. Another said: if you visualize the logo before you start working on it, then all you have to do is execute.
What is one thing you could picture in detail before you start it?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write one task you will do this week.
Write it as a film: where, with what, how it looks.
Write why it matters to you.
Write the decision tree: if this happens, then that.
Write what you will see when it is finished.

check.q: What did I call determining the importance of information?
What did I say happens as emotional engagement rises?
What did a student say about visualizing a logo first?
choices: Then you only have to execute

recap: Picture it vividly. Know why it matters.
